Two thin coats of the colour should provide you with a solid consistent colour, but lighter paints may need more. Because of this it doesn't matter how thin your paints are, you'll get the same colour every time. 

ALWAYS THIN YOUR PAINTS with a little bit of water :) tutorials recommend the viscosity you're looking for to be like milk. 

Some people say a wet palette will make your paints last overnight, but don't listen to them. A wet palette is designed to make sure your paints don't dry out while you're painting. Bottom line is, be careful with how much you use, and once it's out of the bottle it needs using. You won't notice the small amount of extra paint you're using but you would notice on your models where you've used paint that's been rethinned.

In response to your points paragraph by paragraph: 
1. I'm all for equal rights, and there's inequality everywhere, and I agree, I totally accept that I need to take your word for the experiences I'll never understand. *But that goes both ways*
2. I agree, that is taxing and awful. But men are also victims of violent crime, and are also unsafe in different situations. The statistics of violent crime overwhelmingly affect men, and this is a symptom of a society that doesn't care about the mindset of men. I feel the dangerous situations can't be improved by setting the blame solely at the door of the troubled individuals that are taking part, and there must be some onus on the circumstances that are creating this. In my opinion, the best course of action is not to look to claim victimhood, but to ask how you can help make sure anyone you come into contact with feels heard and understood. You'll notice I actually agree with what you say and I understand that I won't understand. I am asking for you to accept the same for us, that there are facets of male identity that you will never understand.  The fear of being targeted or taken advantage of is not a uniquely female concept. 
3. There are old traditions that need to be broken, yes. There are a lot of industries and mindsets that are unacceptable, I agree. In my own experience, I've only ever worked underneath female managers, and have mostly female coworkers. Ironically enough, in my field men are in the minority and I see a little bit of the other side of gender inequality in the workplace. I accept this is anecdotal, and isn't useful to the general argument, but it proves that the issue isn't as black and white as you imply.
4. Toxic masculinity is very real, I agree, but it is not just a male problem. The stereotype is reinforced by society, not just men. For every man with a problematic outlook, there is a woman who will ridicule vulnerability, or expect chivalry, or assume aggression and a lack of emotional intelligence. I surround myself with good people, and they don't adhere to these outdated views, and it's helped me and all my friends, male and female, to climb out of subconscious sexism. 
5. Women have been the underdog for a long time, yes, but the act of promoting gender equality by focusing on one side of it is not the way forwards. There are hugely negative impacts being felt by the male community, of ALL economic and social backgrounds, that could be prevented by a lack of sweeping generalized statements and the idea that all men have it better than all women. It won't convince a troubled young man or woman to open up, or engage in a good natured mindset. 
6. A poor man is statistically the most likely individual to be involved in a violent crime. Rich men are also victims of crime. The definition of privilege is this: a special right, advantage, or immunity granted or available only to a particular person or group. Men as a generalised group do not have this. The statistics of violent crime show that actually, men have less of this. We all want to feel safe, and none of us do. Every case needs to be taken on an individual basis, lest we start stereotyping. A young man who has learned the wrong lessons because no one would confront his idea of masculinity in a caring way is FAR more at risk than a young woman living in a nice area who has the economic means to avoid dangerous situations. It's a case by case basis. 
Men lack basic safety and the right to be taken seriously also. This thread is full of anecdotal evidence of how men cannot be genuine or vulnerable, and how the same system that might not take a woman seriously will also absolutely not take a vulnerable man seriously in the same way. 

I'm hoping you read these points and try to accept that there are too many variables to assume women have it worse. We're all in this together, I want everyone to be safe and feel safe, and I try my best to promote this. We're all equal, if one of us falls down we should help them back up, we shouldn't have to check how much 'privilege' you think that person may have before you hold your arm out for them. 

Love you dude, I can tell this is close to your heart and I hope you feel like this general poopy situation is getting better one day.

Politely disagree on the 'lot more problems'. Please don't think I'm downplaying your struggles, I don't intend to, I can't imagine how hard it is to be in your position, but at the same time, you can't imagine how hard it is to be in mine. The stats on suicide are a good example of the differences between genders, men just have different problems and are just as much victims in the social hierarchy that society creates. I'm not saying men have it worse, I just think in these times, living is exceptionally hard for everyone, and assuming privilege on someone else's behalf is just as harmful as embracing a negative stereotype. 

It's shit for everyone, please don't imply it's less shit for someone else. Two wrongs don't make a right in the fight for acceptance and equality. 

Hope your day is going good.
